# M5 gate (a): spoken form of every equation segment and inline-maths sentence, convention spec 3c
the transformation z equals the fraction x minus mu over sigma, end fraction produces the distribution z distributed as n of 0, 1.
the value x in the given equation comes from a normal distribution with mean mu and standard deviation sigma.
if x is a normally distributed random variable and x distributed as n of mu, sigma, then the z-score is:
z equals the fraction x minus mu over sigma, end fraction
the z-score tells you how many standard deviations the value x is above to the right of or below to the left of the mean, mu.
values of x that are larger than the mean have positive z-scores, and values of x that are smaller than the mean have negative z-scores.
if x equals the mean, then x has a z-score of zero.
suppose x distributed as n of 5, 6.
this says that x is a normally distributed random variable with mean mu equals 5 and standard deviation sigma equals 6.
suppose x equals 17.
z equals the fraction x minus mu over sigma, end fraction equals the fraction 17 minus 5 over 6, end fraction equals 2
this means that x equals 17 is two standard deviations 2 sigma above or to the right of the mean mu equals 5.
notice that: 5 plus 2 times 6 equals 17 the pattern is mu plus z sigma equals x
now suppose x equals 1.
then: z equals the fraction x minus mu over sigma, end fraction equals the fraction 1 minus 5 over 6, end fraction equals minus 0.67 rounded to two decimal places
this means that x equals 1 is 0.67 standard deviations minus 0.67 sigma below or to the left of the mean mu equals 5.
notice that: 5 plus minus 0.67 times 6 is approximately equal to one this has the pattern mu plus minus 0.67 sigma equals 1
summarizing, when z is positive, x is above or to the right of mu and when z is negative, x is to the left of or below mu.
or, when z is positive, x is greater than mu, and when z is negative, x is less than mu.

this z-score tells you that x equals 10 is standard deviations to the right or left of the mean what is the mean?
